title: What Happens When You Type google.com and Press Enter

sections.heading: Everyday analogy - sending a letter
sections.body:
Imagine typing google.com is like mailing a letter.

You write an address (the URL). Your helper (the browser) checks if it is a real address or just a search term. Then it asks a directory (networking) where that address lives, and sends your letter through many hands to the right house (the server).

- URL means the address you type, like google.com.
- Browser is the app that reads and shows web pages.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body:
Engineers ask this question to learn decisions, not just code.

The repo "what-happens-when" breaks the journey into tiny steps: the g key is pressed, the shell receives input, a key event is sent to the app, the URL is parsed, and then browser internals and networking take over.

This teaches how a browser, network, and server work together as one system.

sections.heading: What can go wrong
sections.body:
Each step can fail.

- If URL parsing fails, you search instead of visiting.
- If networking fails, the address cannot be found and the page never loads.
- If the server is busy, it responds slowly or not at all.

Thinking in steps helps you find where a problem started and fix that part first.

steps.narration: You press a key, the keyboard sends a signal.
The app receives a KeyPress event from the system.
Browser checks if your text is a URL or search term.
Browser uses networking to find the server address.
Server gets the request and sends back the page.

quiz.q: What does the browser do first with what you typed?
options: Parse if it is a URL or search term
quiz.why: The save shows Parse URLs and Is it a URL, or a search term as early steps.

quiz.q: Why do engineers study the full what-happens-when flow?
options: To understand decisions across browser, network, and server
quiz.why: The repo teaches engineering reasoning beyond code: browser internals and networking as a system.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x overnight?
quiz.why: Networking and servers get overloaded first when many more requests arrive at once.
